title: Decimal Comparer
context: Grade 5, the pages on comparing and ordering decimals. An adult sees two rules. What the pages are doing is comparing place by place from the left, the whole number parts first, so the first place that differs decides and more digits after the point is not more. Writing zeros to make like decimals is a help for the eye, not a rule.

writeup.why: Compare two decimals by their whole number parts and then place by place, and arrange decimals in ascending or descending order.
writeup.look: Two decimal cards with their points in one line over a place strip, bars to scale on a tape under them, and an ordering ladder on the last phase.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Decimal Comparer' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many places have been compared so far, counting from the left. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The two cards stand at x 110, y 230 and y 320, each 520 wide and 76 tall, their large near-black points on one vertical line at x 330, the digits deep blue, over a place strip at y 410. A pair that matches fades to half strength; the first pair that differs lights amber, labelled Decides, and the sign is written green between the cards at x 680. The tape runs along y 500 from x 110 to x 1030, marked in ones and tenths, with one bar for each card drawn to scale above it. The Make like button sits at x 720, y 230; zeros it writes are violet, labelled Added zero. On the last phase the ordering ladder of four rungs fills the lower half from y 420, each rung 520 wide, with a slot for the sign between every pair and the Ascending and Descending switch at x 720, y 440. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key and the two sign keys, for setting a decimal or typing the greater decimal, a sign or an order into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last ladder in order, each sign between its pair and the deciding places lit.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, when the tenths decide, the bar of the longer decimal shrinks back beside the other with a soft slide, as if it had been caught standing on its toes.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with two decimal cards standing one above the other, their points in one line, and the bars drawn to scale on the tape under them. Nothing is lit. On the fourth phase the cards wait in a row above the empty ordering ladder instead. One thing moves, once: the Compare button, or the first card over the ladder, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.

source_tool.description: Two decimal cards stand one above the other in the upper half of the working area, deep blue, with their points in one vertical line over a place strip naming Tens, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths. A Compare button lights the two digits of one place at a time, starting with the whole number parts; a pair that matches fades to half strength, and the first pair that differs lights amber and is labelled Decides, with the sign written green between the two cards. Under the cards two bars on one tape, marked in ones and tenths, are drawn to scale for the two decimals, so the longer bar is the greater number whatever the number of digits. A Make like button writes violet zeros after the point on the shorter decimal, labelled Added zero, and a note says the zeros are a help, not a rule. On the last phase an ordering ladder of four rungs fills the lower half; decimal cards drag onto its rungs, an Ascending and Descending switch sets which way it runs, and a sign is written between every pair of rungs as the cards land. A number pad sets any decimal with up to three places. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many places have been compared.
source_tool.art_direction: A tape of jumps, compared place by place / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: strips cut into ten equal parts, hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, place value charts with a column for each place, column sums with their points in one line, and measuring jugs, ropes and scales marked in tenths.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared or combined with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip in tenths has ten parts of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
The decimal point is drawn large and always sits between the ones and the tenths. In a column, every point lies on one vertical line.
A place value chart names every column above its digit: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance.

Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a strip cutting into tenths, ten tenths sliding together into one whole, a zero appearing after the point, or a carry moving to the next place.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a decimal plays in a piece of working: every decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it, and every result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum or a difference, is green, with its shaded parts; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Ten of one place traded for one of the next place, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written at the end, after the point, to make like decimals is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. An unshaded part of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the decimal point itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Start from the left. Which place is the first to differ?
voice.onNext: Two new decimals. Look at the whole numbers first.
voice.opening: Two decimals, their points in one line.
voice.onFinish: The first place that differed decided every time.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Compare any decimals, and order any four.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has measured jumps on a tape and circled the first place where two lengths differ. The tool is what walks the places one pair at a time and stops where it is decided, with bars to scale beside the digits.

answer_key.rule: Compare the whole number parts first; the greater whole number part is the greater decimal. If they are the same, compare the tenths, then the hundredths, then the thousandths: the first place that differs decides. More digits after the point does not make a decimal greater. Writing zeros to make like decimals can help line the places up; it is a help, not a rule. Ascending order runs from the smallest to the greatest, and descending order from the greatest to the smallest.
answer_key.wrong: The two cards are compared again pair by pair from the left, and the bars under them are redrawn to scale with the child's choice lit, so the child sees which bar is longer. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Compare the whole number parts first: 15 and 8.
The whole number parts differ, so the digits after the point do not matter.
items.question: Which is greater, 15.2 or 8.96?
items.checkpoint: When the whole number parts differ, the greater whole number part decides.
items.misconception: Choosing 8.96 because it has more digits and bigger digits after the point, though its whole number part is smaller.

steps: The whole number parts are both 6, so compare the tenths.
4 tenths is more than 3 tenths, so 6.4 > 6.38.
Writing 6.4 as 6.40 can help the eye, but it is a help, not a rule.
items.question: Which is greater, 6.38 or 6.4?
items.checkpoint: When the whole number parts are equal, the first place that differs decides.
items.misconception: Choosing 6.38 because 38 is more than 4, which compares the digits after the point as whole numbers.

steps: 0.625 has more digits after the point, but that does not make it greater.
The whole number parts are both 0, so compare the tenths.
7 tenths is more than 6 tenths, so 0.7 > 0.625.
items.question: Which is greater, 0.7 or 0.625?
items.checkpoint: More digits after the point is not more.
items.misconception: Choosing 0.625 because it is longer, which counts digits instead of comparing places.

steps: The whole number parts are all 3, so compare the tenths: 3.9 has 9 tenths and the other two have 0 tenths.
Compare 3.09 and 3.009 at the hundredths: 9 hundredths is more than 0 hundredths.
So in descending order, greatest first, 3.9 > 3.09 > 3.009.
items.question: Put 3.09, 3.9 and 3.009 in descending order.
items.checkpoint: Descending order runs from the greatest to the smallest.
items.misconception: Putting 3.009 first because it has the most digits, which is the ascending end, not the descending one.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Which is greater, 4.53 or 4.51?
items.final_answer: 4.53. The ones and the tenths match, and 3 hundredths is more than 1 hundredth

items.question: Which is greater, 0.8 or 0.79?
items.final_answer: 0.8, because 8 tenths is more than 7 tenths

items.question: One ribbon is 2.64 m long and another is 2.6 m long. Which is longer?
items.final_answer: The 2.64 m ribbon. The ones and the tenths match, and 4 hundredths is more than 0 hundredths

items.question: Which is greater, 0.6 or 0.587?
items.final_answer: 0.6, because 6 tenths is more than 5 tenths

items.question: Which is greater, 30.001 or 29.999?
items.final_answer: 30.001, because 30 > 29. The digits after the point do not matter

teaching_notes: Look at the whole number parts first; if they differ, the comparison is over. Then compare place by place from the tenths, and the first place that differs decides. More digits after the point does not mean greater: set nine tenths beside three hundred forty-five thousandths on two grids. Writing zeros to make like decimals helps the eye line the places up, and it is a help, not a rule. When ordering, write the sign between every pair.
generation_prompt: Build a decimal comparing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Two deep blue decimal cards stand one above the other with their points in one vertical line over a place strip. A Compare button lights the digits of one place at a time from the left, whole number parts first; a matching pair fades to half strength and the first pair that differs lights amber, labelled Decides, with the sign written green between the cards. Under the cards two bars on one tape marked in ones and tenths are drawn to scale. A Make like button writes violet zeros after the point, labelled Added zero, with a note that it is a help, not a rule. On the last phase an ordering ladder of four rungs takes cards by drag, an Ascending and Descending switch sets its direction, and a sign is written between every pair. A number pad. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of places compared. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right.
